sentences.text: A ptarmigan in winter is white, and this is the least interesting thing about a ptarmigan.
Isla's great-grandmother had made this point to her at least thirteen times, always in the same slightly irritated tone, as though somebody had just that moment suggested otherwise.
Lots of things are white in the snow.
The hare goes white.
The stoat goes white.
Being white is easy and it does not work very well, because snow is not one colour and a white thing on it casts a shadow and has an edge.
Isla had been made to prove this to herself at about eight, on the slope behind the house, with a white plastic bag and a good deal of complaining.
Her great-grandmother had put the bag in the snow forty metres off and told her to find it, and Isla had found it in under two seconds and had said so, at some volume.
"Aye," the old woman had said.
"That's white.

Now find the bird." What the ptarmigan does is different, and Isla did not properly understand it until she was eleven and had spent forty minutes on the ridge above Cnoc Dubh looking directly at a bird she had been told was four metres away.
They do not hide themselves.
They hide.
They sit in a scoop in the lee of a stone, where the light is already flat, and they do not move at all, and the not-moving is not stillness — it is a positive act, sustained, for hours.
Everything about the animal is arranged to remove the two things an eye is actually looking for, which are the outline and the change.
The feathers go right down over the feet so there are no legs to make a line.
The black tail is tucked.
The eye, which is the one thing that cannot be white, is held behind the rock.
And when you do finally see one, you cannot then un-see it, and you sit there feeling foolish, and seventeen metres away there is another one you also cannot see.
The moment of seeing is the strangest part and it does not get less strange with practice.

There is nothing there, and there is nothing there, and there is nothing there — and then there is a bird, entire, obvious, four metres away, in a place your eye has crossed perhaps two hundred times in the last half hour.
Nothing has changed.
The bird did not move; that is precisely what it has been not doing.
What changed is on your side, and it happens all at once, and it cannot be undone: once you have seen that bird you will see it every time you look at it for the rest of the afternoon.
Which means, and Isla worked this out on the ridge at eleven with her hands going numb, that the entire trick is being run against something in your head rather than against your eyes.
"That," said her great-grandmother, "is the whole business.
It is not about looking like snow.
It is about not being findable." She was ninety-four that year.
She had been eleven herself in 1953.
